description: Muslim teaching on marriage, sexual relationships, family life, and the support of the ummah.
content_html:
Marriage in Islam

Marriage (nikah) is considered a fundamental Islamic institution. It is an act of worship and a sunna (practice) of the Prophet Muhammad, who is reported in hadith to have described marriage as “half of the deen (religion).” Surah 4 (An-Nisa, “the Women”) is the primary Qur’anic source for marriage law and ethics. It establishes rights and responsibilities between spouses, the conditions for valid marriage, and the framework for family life. Marriage in Islam is not a sacrament (as in Catholicism) but a legal contract (aqd) which, when entered into freely and with proper conditions, is pleasing to Allah and an expression of permissible love.

The purposes of Islamic marriage include companionship and emotional fulfilment, procreation, the strengthening of the ummah, and the channelling of sexual desire within a relationship approved by Allah. Cohabitation (living together outside marriage) is not accepted in Islamic teaching — sexual relationships outside marriage are regarded as morally wrong. Non-religious Humanists and atheists generally argue that committed relationships have equal value whether legally formalised or not; Muslims respond that the framework of marriage provides the security, commitment and public accountability that children and partners deserve.

Key Fact

Surah 4 (An-Nisa, “the Women”) is the primary Qur’anic source for marriage law and family ethics. Marriage in Islam is a legal contract (nikah) that channels sexual desire within Allah’s approved framework and serves the purpose of procreation, companionship and strengthening the ummah.

Sexual Relationships

Muslim teaching is clear that sexual relationships are only appropriate within marriage. Surah 23:5–11 praises the believers who “guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess — for then they are not blameworthy.” This passage establishes the marital context as the only acceptable framework for sexual activity. Muslims believe this protects individuals from exploitation, ensures children are born into committed families, and reflects the divine order for human sexuality.

On same-sex relationships, classical Islamic jurisprudence regards these as impermissible, drawing on Qur’anic and hadith sources. This is a matter of significant debate in contemporary Islam: a small number of modern Muslim scholars and communities argue for a reinterpretation, but the mainstream Sunni and Shi’a scholarly tradition maintains the prohibition. Non-religious Humanists argue that loving, committed relationships between consenting adults are morally equal regardless of gender. Muslim responses emphasise that Islamic ethics are grounded in revelation rather than evolving social norms, and that human dignity requires a framework of divine guidance.

Within the Sunni tradition, all four main schools of law (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali) agree on the fundamental permissibility of temporary marriage (mut’ah) being forbidden, while they permit standard nikah. Shi’a Muslims, particularly Twelver Shi’as, permit mut’ah (temporary marriage for a specified period), which Sunnis do not accept. This divergence reflects deeper differences between Sunni and Shi’a jurisprudence and interpretation of the Prophet’s practice. In questions of polygyny (a man marrying up to four wives, subject to strict conditions), Surah 4:3 permits it “if you fear you cannot be just, then [marry] only one” — most contemporary Muslim families in the West are monogamous in practice, reflecting both local legal norms and a stricter reading of the “justice” condition.

The Purpose and Importance of the Family

The family is central to Islamic life. Surah 46:15–18 instructs children to honour their parents and describes the duty of care for ageing parents as an obligation. Procreation is an important purpose of marriage: the Muslim family is the unit through which the ummah is perpetuated and in which children are raised in the Islamic faith. Children have responsibilities to their parents and parents to their children; the family unit is the primary institution of social support, education and welfare in Islamic teaching.

Islamic family structures have traditionally been extended: grandparents, parents and children living together or in very close proximity, providing mutual support and ensuring that elderly members are cared for within the family rather than delegated to state institutions. The nuclear family structure common in the West is accepted but not ideally preferred — the extended family model better reflects Islamic values of kinship solidarity. The ummah extends the circle of support still further — the mosque community provides resources, counselling, childcare, and support for widows and orphans.

The Support of the Ummah

Surah 3:102–105 calls on believers to “hold fast to the rope of Allah and be not divided among yourselves” — a powerful image of the ummah as a single community bound together by faith, responsible for one another’s wellbeing. The mosque community supports families through rites of passage (Aqiqah at birth, nikah ceremonies, funeral prayers), Islamic education for children (maktab or madrasah), and financial support through Zakah and voluntary charitable networks. Blended and single-parent families are supported by the ummah with the same pastoral concern, recognising that diverse family structures exist in 21st-century society.

Key Fact

Surah 3:102–105 calls believers to “hold fast to the rope of Allah” and not be divided. The ummah is a community of mutual responsibility. The mosque supports families through rites of passage, Islamic education, Zakah distribution, and pastoral care for the vulnerable.
exam_tip_html: Key sources for this lesson: Surah 4 (An-Nisa) for marriage; Surah 23:5–11 for sexual relationships; Surah 46:15–18 for family duties; Surah 3:102–105 for ummah support. Use surah number and verse range in the 5-mark source question. For the 12-mark Discuss on marriage and sexual ethics, you must develop the non-religious (Humanist) counter-argument fully, not just mention it in one sentence. On same-sex relationships, describe the mainstream Muslim position without editorialising — present it as believers hold it. Do not attribute Western social attitudes to all Muslims. SPaG: nikah, ummah, procreation, An-Nisa.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Marriage (nikah) is an act of worship and legal contract in Islam — Surah 4 (An-Nisa) is the primary Qur’anic source. Its purposes include procreation, companionship, and strengthening the ummah. Cohabitation and sexual activity outside marriage are not permitted.
  • Surah 23:5–11 restricts sexual activity to marriage. Classical Islamic jurisprudence regards same-sex relationships as impermissible, though this is debated in contemporary Muslim scholarship. Surah 46:15–18 establishes children’s duties to their parents.
  • Surah 3:102–105 calls the ummah to hold together and support one another — the mosque community provides rites of passage, Islamic education, Zakah distribution, and pastoral care for all family structures.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the purpose of marriage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: procreation — bringing children into the world and raising them in the faith (1); companionship and emotional fulfilment between spouses (1); strengthening the ummah — the worldwide Muslim community is built through faithful families (1). Other valid purposes accepted.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the ummah supports Muslim families.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the mosque community provides rites of passage (Aqiqah, nikah ceremonies, funeral prayers) (1); madrasah (Islamic school) provides religious education for children (1); Zakah and sadaqah provide financial support for those in need within the community (1). Other valid support mechanisms accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe sexual relationships should only take place within marriage.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Surah 23:5-11 teaches that believers 'guard their private parts' except within marriage — sex outside this framework is regarded as transgressing divinely set limits, which Muslims believe leads to individual and social harm (2); marriage provides the committed, legally binding context in which children can be raised securely — ensuring procreation takes place within a stable family unit as Allah intended (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim teachings about the purpose of the family, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Surah 46:15-18 teaches that children must honour their parents and care for them as they age — the family is the unit of mutual obligation across generations, not just between parents and young children (2); Surah 3:102-105 calls the ummah to hold fast to Allah's rope and not be divided — families are strengthened by embedding them in the mosque community, which provides mutual support (2); source credit for Surah 4, Surah 46:15-18, or Surah 3:102-105 named with verse numbers (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Muslim teaching on marriage is too restrictive for the 21st century.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Counter case: Humanists argue consensual relationships have equal value without marriage; same-sex relationships are excluded by classical jurisprudence; cohabitation is a normal feature of modern society. Muslim case: Surah 4, Surah 23:5-11 — marriage provides security, procreation within a committed framework, and reflects divine guidance that transcends shifting social norms; ummah support (Surah 3:102-105) shows the communal context. Evaluate: is the 'too restrictive' charge based on assuming a particular cultural standard as the norm? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: nikah, ummah, procreation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Sunni and Shi'a Islam differ in their understanding of marriage, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Shi'a Muslims (particularly Twelver Shi'as) permit temporary marriage (mut'ah) for a specified period, while Sunni Muslims regard this as forbidden on the basis that the Prophet abolished it — this is a significant point of divergence in Islamic marriage law (2); all four Sunni schools and Shi'a jurisprudence agree that the nikah contract requires the free consent of both parties — Surah 4 provides the Qur'anic framework for marriage rights and responsibilities that both traditions draw on (2); source credit for Surah 4 named explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does Surah 23:5-11 teach about sexual relationships?
options: Sexual relationships are permissible between any consenting adults
Believers guard their private parts except within marriage
Sexual activity is discouraged even within marriage
Marriage is only necessary for those who cannot control their desires

knowledge_checks.q: What does Surah 3:102-105 teach about the ummah?
options: Each Muslim community should operate independently of others
Believers should hold fast to the rope of Allah and not be divided among themselves
Only scholars may lead the Muslim community
The ummah is defined by national identity rather than shared faith

knowledge_checks.q: Surah 4 is also known as An-Nisa, which means 'the _____' in Arabic.
The strengthening of the _____ — the worldwide Muslim community — is one of the key purposes of Islamic marriage and family life.
Match each Qur'anic source to its teaching on marriage or family:
right: Primary source for marriage law and spousal rights
Believers guard their private parts except within marriage
Children must honour their parents and care for them as they age

flashcard_questions.q: What is nikah in Islamic teaching?
flashcard_questions.a: A legal contract (marriage) between a Muslim man and woman, understood as both a legal agreement and an act of worship.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Surah 4 also called, and why is it important for marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: An-Nisa ('the Women') — the primary Qur'anic source for marriage law, spousal rights and family ethics.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 23:5-11 teach about sexual relationships?
flashcard_questions.a: Believers 'guard their private parts' except within marriage — sexual activity outside marriage transgresses divine limits.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 46:15-18 say about family duties?
flashcard_questions.a: Children must honour their parents and care for them as they age — a multigenerational obligation of support.
The worldwide community of Muslims — all those who submit to Allah, regardless of nationality or ethnicity.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 3:102-105 say about the ummah?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Hold fast to the rope of Allah and be not divided' — the ummah is a single community of mutual responsibility.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Shi'a view on mut'ah (temporary marriage)?
flashcard_questions.a: Twelver Shi'a Muslims permit it for a specified period; Sunnis regard it as forbidden.

flashcard_questions.q: What is procreation as a purpose of Islamic marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: Bringing children into the world and raising them in the Islamic faith — perpetuating the ummah.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the mosque community support Muslim families?
flashcard_questions.a: Through rites of passage, Islamic education (madrasah), Zakah distribution, and pastoral care.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Islamic teaching on cohabitation?
flashcard_questions.a: Not accepted — sexual relationships outside marriage are regarded as morally wrong; the nikah contract provides the proper framework.

glossary_terms.definition: A binding contract (nikah) between a Muslim man and woman, understood as both a legal agreement and an act of worship pleasing to Allah.
The worldwide community of Muslims — all those who submit to Allah, regardless of nationality or ethnicity.
Bringing children into the world and raising them in the faith — one of the primary purposes of Islamic marriage.
Sexual or romantic relationships between two people of the same sex — not permitted in classical Islamic jurisprudence.
A family consisting of parents and their children without extended kin — accepted but not preferred over the extended family model in Islamic teaching.
A family formed when two adults with children from previous relationships come together — supported by the ummah's pastoral care.

hero_image_caption: A Muslim family at the mosque — marriage, family and the ummah as interconnected pillars of Islamic life
